newsitem.title: USA: HK future leader Tung pledges to protect rights.
newsitem.headline: HK future leader Tung pledges to protect rights.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa pledged on Tuesday to protect the right to protest and vowed that no Tiananmen Square-style massacre would take place under his leadership when the British colony reverts to Chinese rule.

"Demonstration is part of our culture, demonstration is part of life ... they will be free to demonstrate as they please, but I would hope they would abide by the laws of Hong Kong if they wish to do so," Tung said in an interview on the ABC News programme "Nightline."
Rights groups and academics have warned of threats to freedom and civil liberties when Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30 after 156 years under the British flag.
Tung said anyone should "feel comfortable to demonstrate" after July 1, adding: "If they want to be martyrs, they will be very disappointed."

Asked if the 1989 massacre in Beijing's Tiananmen Square -- when Beijing crushed the student-led pro-democracy movement -- could be repeated in Hong Kong, Tung replied: "No, it can't happen here. It will not happen here. I will not allow it to happen here."

"Insofar as Hong Kong is concerned, we are living in a very different world, we have a culture which has demonstrations almost every day, we have people voicing different views everywhere," Tung said.

Tung has launched a major "consultation" on the future of political freedom, asking members of the public and organisations to submit views on his plan to require police approval for protests and to ban foreign funding of political groups.

Pro-democracy parties, lawyers, human rights groups, Western-style trade unions and churches have all vigorously objected to the plan in written submissions. Government officials in Washington and London also have criticised it.
But groups representing industry, commerce, pro-China political parties and pro-Beijing trade unions support Tung's plan, which was forced on him in March by a Chinese parliamentary resolution.

Tung, who stepped from the helm of his family's shipping empire into the glare of the political spotlight when a Beijing-backed committee chose him to run Hong Kong, said in the ABC interview he was "a reluctant candidate."
"Duty beckoned. I am now doing it. I now will do the best for Hong Kong," he said.
